#5978. Democrats Have a Historic Opportunity to Rethink Capitalism

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Democrats Have a Historic Opportunity to Rethink Capitalism

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

“The barbarians are inside the gate,” Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson wrote on X in July in the wake of a slew of primary victories by progressive candidates. By splitting the Democratic Party and inviting the ire of Republicans, these insurgents became a defining force in the U.S. midterms, with candidates such as James Talarico and Annie Andrews winning unlikely Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina, and Peggy Flanagan and Manny Rutinel clinching victories in Minnesota and Colorado, respectively. The formal adoption of a resolution condemning socialism recently in the House of Representatives and U.S. President Donald Trump’s warnings about the “communist menace” as fundamentally un-American on the country’s 250th anniversary signal how seriously the challenge was taken this past summer, even as—amid an ongoing cost-of-living crisis and growing disillusionment with the economic system—the concept of democratic socialism has become more palatable to American voters.

The verdict at the polls this week is a referendum on not just a highly consequential political contest, but also a historic battle of ideas. Having breached the gates, can this new wave of progressives change the architecture of U.S. capitalism?

“The barbarians are inside the gate,” Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson wrote on X in July in the wake of a slew of primary victories by progressive candidates. By splitting the Democratic Party and inviting the ire of Republicans, these insurgents became a defining force in the U.S. midterms, with candidates such as James Talarico and Annie Andrews winning unlikely Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina, and Peggy Flanagan and Manny Rutinel clinching victories in Minnesota and Colorado, respectively. The formal adoption of a resolution condemning socialism recently in the House of Representatives and U.S. President Donald Trump’s warnings about the “communist menace” as fundamentally un-American on the country’s 250th anniversary signal how seriously the challenge was taken this past summer, even as—amid an ongoing cost-of-living crisis and growing disillusionment with the economic system—the concept of democratic socialism has become more palatable to American voters.

The verdict at the polls this week is a referendum on not just a highly consequential political contest, but also a historic battle of ideas. Having breached the gates, can this new wave of progressives change the architecture of U.S. capitalism?

On the left, politicians associated with democratic socialism, most prominently New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, have revived ideas once consigned to the margins—stronger labor institutions, higher minimum wages, universal healthcare, higher taxes, and a wider social safety net including paid family leave and government-funded preschool and college. At least 11 midterm races were decided on these issues, including the closely watched Senate race in Michigan won by Abdul El-Sayed.

But on the right, Trump, too, by introducing tariffs and returning to industrial policy, has thrown the conventional economic playbook out the window and eschewed the free-trade impulses that traditionally characterized Republican economics.

The two movements are perceived to be almost completely at odds. But what unites them is that they are—fundamentally—reactions to the economic consensus that has been dominant since the Cold War. Former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who along with former U.S. President Ronald Reagan ushered in capitalism’s era of dominance, described its global embrace with the pithy phrase: “There is no alternative.”

The political scientist Francis Fukuyama subsequently coined a grand formulation to describe the alliance between free market economics and liberal democracy as an elixir of economic and political life: the “end of history.” The economic proposition that underlay it, known as neoclassical economics, proposed to replace the faltering human touch with the “invisible hand.” Built around the belief that markets could coordinate millions of strangers, it promised to convert private interest into public benefit. Without requiring shared values or common purpose, it not only relied on the rationality of the price mechanism to allocate every resource to its best use but also promised to diminish inequality.

The system succeeded in delivering global growth on an unprecedented scale, roughly tripling  the world economy in size, yet the model’s blind spots have become increasingly harder to ignore. The imperfections of the price mechanism that treats carbon as a negative externality and children a positive one, but fails to put a value on either, are becoming more glaring. Collective-action problems, such as the alignment problem presented by artificial intelligence and climate change, demonstrate that individually rational choices can produce collective outcomes that are highly irrational. And inequality has increased, particularly within countries, even as aggregate output has grown.

Most fundamentally, around the world, the human psyche is instinctively rejecting the desiccated account of human nature as solitary and narrowly self-interested, on which economics is premised, and the institutions built around these assumptions that leave people feeling increasingly alienated.

Unsurprisingly, Gallup finds that confidence in U.S. institutions is near an all-time low. In that sense, both the populist right and the progressive left are rebellions against the attempt to shoehorn humans into the role of the relentlessly utility-maximizing Homo Economicus, or Economic Man, at the heart of the narrative of economics.

Flesh-and-blood people may respond to incentives, but they equally value emotion and social connection. Yet capitalism’s scaling logic has relentlessly favored speed and size. The result has been banks that are too big to fail, “Big Tech” that concentrates power and sets off antitrust alarms, and global supply chains whose efficiency can tip rapidly into fragility. The drive for economic growth quickly outpaces the human capacity for trust.

By contrast with the proportions of most of our economic institutions, the famous Dunbar number shows that each human being can sustain roughly 150 stable relationships. At the same time, a growing body of research establishes that cooperation and reciprocity are economically salient patterns of behavior defining our relationships.

Our institutions are simultaneously too small to contend with problems on a global or planetary scale—think of climate change, artificial general intelligence, financial contagion, global poverty, and pandemics—and so are, ethically and functionally, suboptimal on a cognitive level. Yet our nation-states, domestic economies, and corporations are too large to feel affectively meaningful.

So, what if, instead of building ever-larger institutions ever faster, we built “affective institutions” that acknowledge the human capacity for fellow feeling, engage the “moral machinery” or finer feelings, and aggregate them into consensus-based communities?

Elinor Ostrom’s Nobel Prize-winning scholarship illustrates, through examples such as forests, fisheries, and irrigation systems around the world, that community governance structures can rival markets and governments by deploying locally constructed norms to create robust economic communities.

Her findings are often considered quaint because of the constraint on institutional size that they impose, but new breakthroughs in network science provide a possible answer to the problem of scale. Dense communities where reputation and repeated interaction matter can be linked through threads or bridges that connect those communities, allowing information, capital, and successful practices to travel between them. The resulting architecture is a latticework of fishnets connected through fireworks, a system that is cohesive but not centralized, balancing local trust and large-scale reach.

Real-world models of what these “affective institutions” might look like already exist. Mondragon’s cooperatives in the Basque region of Spain combine locally governed, largely autonomous enterprises embedded in a shared financial structure. The group employed more than 71,000 people and recorded more than $12 billion in sales in 2025, serving as a significant proof of concept.

The 27-country-strong European Union, whose membership includes previously warring nations, represents a much larger, more ambitious experiment. Indeed, its structure, based on the principle of subsidiarity—which holds that decisions should remain at national, regional, or local level unless they can be achieved more effectively at the EU level because of their scale or effects—suggests a more useful economic approach than whether government should be bigger or smaller: At what level should each problem be solved, and how should those levels connect?

This new blueprint is of direct relevance to progressives across the United States. After America’s socialist summer, the question is whether the collective effervescence of the movement can congeal into something that can be sustained.

If the “warmth of collectivism” spreading from New York’s experiment with Zohranomics is to spark a revolution that tackles not just the crisis of affordability but also human agency, then the right scaling technology, built around citizens, consensus, and resilience, will be key. The midterms present a historic opportunity to turn widespread voter disaffection away from the self-destructive nihilism of the Make America Great Again movement and toward constructive agency. That will require moving beyond the stale market-versus-state binary and building structures rooted in individuals, embedded in communities, and linked through diffuse but connected networks. The scientific breakthrough has already happened; the politics just needs to catch up.

Few projects could be more faithful to the American promise than putting people—and the relationships between them—back at the center of economic and social life. Progressives now have a chance to stop being cast as the “barbarians at the gate” and storm the political citadel instead. But to do that, they will need to remodel the architecture of U.S. capitalism, by human hand.

They should reclaim key parts of Joe Biden’s record, rather than run from it.

#5977. 15 lessons from the midterms as Democrats rebound with historic wave

ANALYSIS — It wasn’t exactly a surprise that Democrats did well on Tuesday, but the breadth and depth of their victory was stunning. Votes are still being counted, but it’s looking like a massive blue wave with very few Republican survivors.

Just two years ago, Donald Trump delivered one of the biggest Republican victories in recent history. The GOP won back the White House, finished ahead in the national popular vote, recaptured the Senate majority and held on to the House. But what Republicans thought was a permanent realignment of the party coalitions crumbled under the weight of an unpopular war in the Middle East and voter frustrations over the economy and president’s economic policies.

The complete analysis will come in the weeks and months ahead, but here are a few initial thoughts.

Trump is a political mortal. Despite the pervasive narrative that normal political rules don’t apply to the president, election night showed that is simply not true. Sure, he was a surprise victor in 2016, but as an unpopular sitting president in 2018, his party lost a net of 40 House seats. When he ran for reelection in 2020, again as an unpopular president, he lost. When he got to run against an unpopular Democratic administration in 2024, he won again. And when his job approval rating sank to historic lows, his party was routed in the midterms.

Polls pointed in the right direction. Despite a decade of ridicule and abuse, the polling industry had a good cycle. Of course, there were a few outliers, but much of the public and private data (at least on the Democratic side) pointed to a good midterm for Democrats. Surprise outcomes on Tuesday were likely more due to a lack of data than poor data. And, if anything, some surveys underestimated the support for Democratic candidates. Pollsters still have methodological challenges, particularly with low response rates, but it’s time to ditch the narrative that polls always underestimate Republicans.

Democrats captured the Senate. Democrats are going to gain at least seven Senate seats: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. They might gain up to nine with wins in Alaska and Mississippi. (Both races haven’t been called as yet by The Associated Press). They needed to gain four seats for a majority. Our projection of a Democratic gain of four to six seats was directionally accurate but will fall at least slightly below the final tally.

It could have been worse for Republicans. While it’s almost hard to believe, the night could have been a bigger catastrophe for the Senate GOP. Louisiana Rep. Julia Letlow won the open seat by 2 points; appointed Florida Sen. Ashley Moody won by 3 points; and Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts was leading by 7 points as of Wednesday morning. If Sens. Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi or Dan Sullivan of Alaska survive, they’d do so by narrow margins. Meanwhile, Democrats didn’t really have any close calls, as they held Michigan (6 points as of Wednesday morning), Minnesota (10 points), New Hampshire (14 points) and Georgia (18 points).

Democrats captured the House. While dozens of races remain uncalled by the AP, Democrats will gain the House majority as expected. But the size of the wave is going to be bigger than expected. Democrats will likely clear our projection of a net gain of 20 to 30 seats and could approach their 40-seat gain during Trump’s first midterm.

Redistricting flopped for Republicans. Republicans are struggling to gain any of the seats they intentionally redrew to elect new members of their own party. Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas ended up as debacles for the GOP with near total domination by Democrats up and down the ballot, all in states Trump won just two years ago. North Carolina Republican Tim Moore is on track to lose a district that he helped draw for himself.

It didn’t have to be this way. Even though Republicans are placing the early blame on history and inevitability, Tuesday’s results were not a foregone conclusion. Things could have been very different had Trump not started the conflict with Iran, which resulted in domestic economic hardship, or waged a tariff war with friendly countries. Or if he had limited his immigration policy to closing the border and deporting violent criminals in the country illegally. Republicans would have held the Senate, and it would have been an extremely close fight for the House. No matter who or what Republicans choose to blame, the party is here because of Trump.

Sometimes history repeats itself. Twenty years ago, there was an unpopular Republican president in the White House with a war in the Middle East that was driving up fuel prices. Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress as Republicans lost 30 House seats and six Senate seats — a remarkably similar outcome to this cycle.

Midterms portend the future, except when they don’t. Democrats had a great night this week but that’s no guarantee the success will continue. In their best-case scenario, 2026 could be the first part of a two-cycle wave, similar to 2006 and 2008, when Democrats expanded their House majority and won the White House. But 2028 could also look like 2012 in reverse, with Republicans bouncing back from a disastrous midterm as Democrats did after the 2010 tea party wave.

Candidate quality is only a fraction of the story. Republicans can try to blame their candidates or campaigns, whether it’s Hyde-Smith, Ken Paxton in Texas or Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, but all of them would have won in a political environment in which the president was even modestly popular. Without Trump’s self-inflicted policy wounds, candidate quality would not have mattered as much for Republicans, and they could have exploited Democrats with vulnerabilities, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Gina Hinojosa’s victory over GOP Greg Abbott in Texas, where Democrats also appear on track to sweep every other statewide race, is proof that Republican problems in the Lone Star State extended beyond Paxton’s baggage.

The Trump coalition collapsed. The coalition that brought Republicans to the mountaintop didn’t stick around very long as the party lost ground among a host of key demographic groups that were supposed to be a permanent part of its voter bloc. Trump finished behind Kamala Harris by just 11 points among voters aged 18-29. Republican candidates lost those voters by 47 points on Tuesday, according to the exit polls. Trump finished 5 points behind Harris among Latino voters, but Republicans lost them by 27 points this year. Trump lagged Harris by just 3 points among independent voters but Republicans lost them by 17 points this week. Trump bested Harris among male voters by 12 points in 2024, but Republicans ran even with Democrats with this group on Tuesday. Republicans even lost ground among voters without a college degree. Trump was +13 against Harris in 2024, but Republicans were just +4 in the midterms.

Personal brands matter until they don’t. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania’s 1st District came into the cycle with stellar reputations about bucking partisan trends, but both Republicans went down to defeat. Rep. Mike Lawler of New York’s 17th could join them. It’s just evidence that voters have a limited tolerance for voting against their own partisan tendencies.

Pay attention to special elections. For two years, Democratic candidates significantly overperformed in special elections and regularly scheduled off-year elections. Republicans dismissed the results as “special,” finding excuses to explain them away. But that was a mistake. Their turnout problem was right in front of everyone for more than a year.

Elections are humbling. Losing twice to Trump was a humbling experience for Democrats. Seeing most of those gains wiped out in a single night should be humbling for Republicans. But we’ll see what lessons each party chooses to take from these results.

White evangelicals couldn’t save Republicans. White evangelical voters continue to be one of the most reliable pieces of the GOP coalition. After supporting Trump with 76 percent in 2020 and 82 percent in 2024, and Republican candidates with 83 percent in 2022, white evangelicals supported GOP candidates once again, with 82 percent. But turnout did not keep pace. According to the exit polls, white evangelicals made up 17 percent of the midterm electorate after consistently comprising around a quarter of voters for more than a decade.

#5976. What Israel’s Election Won’t Change

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ALUF BENN is Editor in Chief of Haaretz and a Senior Fellow at the Bill Graham Centre for Contemporary International History at the University of Toronto.

The Constraints and Costs of the New Security Consensus

When Israelis go to the polls on October 27, much of the world will be rooting for the defeat of the country’s longtime prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Under his nearly two decades of rule, Israel has become steadily more aggressive. It has abandoned any pretense of supporting a two-state solution; started constructing hundreds of new Jewish settlements in the West Bank; and, following Hamas’s cross-border attack on October 7, 2023, laid waste to the Gaza Strip, occupied parts of Lebanon and Syria, and launched war against Iran, its archnemesis. Meanwhile, its democratic institutions have faced endless attacks by Netanyahu and his allies, who have proposed laws that would, among other things, greatly curtail the power of Israel’s courts. Should he return to power for an unprecedented seventh term, many fret that the country will permanently transition into a rogue theocratic actor.

To many voters, this election thus marks a crucial turning point in Israeli domestic policy. The prime minister’s main political opponent, former Israel Defense Forces Chief Gadi Eisenkot, holds a more liberal worldview than his competitor. He supports an independent judiciary, a free press, and a professional civil service. Should he win, he will likely try to reverse Netanyahu’s efforts to curtail each institution’s independence.

But an Eisenkot victory is unlikely to change Israel’s foreign policy or approach to the Palestinians. Almost all of Israel’s Jewish political parties, Eisenkot’s included, are opposed to Palestinian statehood, not just Netanyahu’s Likud. They all believe that Israel’s brutal war on Gaza was morally just and practically necessary. And almost all of them think that Israel was right to attack Iran and to establish and create what its government and military call “security zones”—occupied territory—in Lebanon and Syria. In fact, the only real disagreement between Eisenkot and Netanyahu on matters of security is whether the latter made the right tactical decisions in each of these conflicts, such as when Netanyahu rejected a cease-fire in Gaza that would have freed Israeli hostages earlier.

That is not to say he will follow exactly the same course. Eisenkot and Netanyahu differ in important ways on the barrage of West Bank settler attacks against helpless Palestinians, which are aimed at driving them out of their land. The prime minister, committed to his far-right allies, shrugs off the issue, whereas his competitor calls their behavior “Jewish terror.” Even if Eisenkot has little pity for the Palestinian victims, he realizes that the West Bank is on the verge of a bloody explosion and that Israel is at risk of even greater international opprobrium because of its reckless policy there. But overall, no matter what happens in the elections, Israel will continue to repress the Palestinians and strike its enemies. It will thus face diplomatic and economic costs, as the country’s frustrated partners begin cutting off aid and perhaps even enacting sanctions.

There are many issues at play in Israel’s election. Politicians, for example, have debated ultra-Orthodox exemptions from the draft, Netanyahu’s corruption charges, and what, if anything, the government should do about Jewish terrorism. But on the whole, the contest has been focused on who is to blame for failing to stop Hamas’s October 7 attack, which killed 1,200 Israelis and resulted in 251 more being taken hostage in one day. The opposition has argued that Netanyahu is responsible for the country’s worst-ever security failure, pointing out that he sustained Hamas with Qatari money, ignored intelligence warnings about Hamas plots, and then blocked an independent investigation into what happened. Eisenkot, who lost a son and two nephews to fighting in Gaza, has been particularly unsparing in his criticism, repeatedly hammering Netanyahu for refusing to take any accountability for the calamity. The prime minister and his supporters, for their part, have brushed off these accusations. Instead, they have blamed October 7 on the military and security services. They have also promoted conspiracy theories that there is what Netanyahu’s cronies and supporters call “treason from within”—or that someone inside Israel helped facilitate Hamas’s brief invasion.

But despite this blame game, both sides agree on the tragedy’s primary lessons: that Israel is surrounded by diehard merciless enemies and that the Palestinians can never be trusted. This attitude is, in part, a raw expression of anti-Arab racism, which is more visible in Israel’s post–October 7 Jewish society. But it is also an electoral play. If the polling is correct, Eisenkot will need the support, however tacit, of Israel’s two Arab parties to put together a government. Netanyahu is thus trying to win over voters who, much as they hate him personally, cannot stand the idea of a government propped up by Palestinians.

This strategy is unlikely to work on liberal Israelis, who view this election as the last chance to save their homeland from sliding into dictatorship. Many Israelis who live abroad, including immigrants who left the country because of Netanyahu’s leadership, thus intend to come home and vote for his replacement. But these election day visitors and likeminded liberal voters are rallying to protect and preserve their way of life in a country that is becoming more religious and nationalistic. And even many of the anti-Netanyahu voters would be unhappy about partnering with the Arab parties to replace the current government. Few would bother to think about the two-state solution, viewing the idea as a relic from the overly optimistic 1990s. Eisenkot, the current leader of this electorate, has declared his personal opposition to a Palestinian state, as have Israel’s other centrist and conservative opposition figures. Only Yair Golan, the leader of Israel’s sole left-wing Jewish party, supports what he calls “separation from the Palestinians” and a return to diplomacy—and even he lacks a plan for how to make that happen.

In one sense, the country’s rejection of a two-state solution is not new. The last detailed negotiations over Palestinian statehood took place in early 2001. Most Jewish Israelis turned against the idea following the second intifada and Hamas’s 2007 takeover of Gaza. Netanyahu has railed against Palestinian sovereignty for his entire political career. (His brief ostensible endorsement of such a state, in 2009, was heavily conditioned and widely considered insincere.) And after October 7, opposition to the notion has become far more resolute. Before the attack, some major Jewish parties would still pay lip service to the notion of making peace with the Palestinians, and their politicians expressed tentative openness to a settlement. Now, they either reject it out of hand or simply dismiss the issue altogether.

Israeli officials have also become far more aggressive. The country may have turned against Palestinian independence years ago, but for most of the last two decades, it avoided full-scale wars and preserved the low-cost status quo. That restraint, even if disrupted by periodic rounds of fighting with Hamas, endeared Netanyahu to mainstream Israelis, who could pretend that the conflict was a thing of the past and all but forget about the Palestinians. Yet this attitude changed when Hamas crossed the border. Afterward, Israel adopted its current policy of destruction and occupation—which Netanyahu’s election campaign is bragging about, since it knows that bombing Iran and invading Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria have been extremely popular among the population at large. The prime minister’s main opponents all endorsed these tactics—criticizing him only for failing to achieve his pledge of “total victory.”

Netanyahu, in turn, blamed Eisenkot for being soft on Hamas when he served in the country’s war cabinet. Eisenkot then said that he had voted for a more aggressive invasion than what the prime minister ultimately undertook. Eisenkot later pledged to “end Hamas rule in Gaza within 18 months” if elected. This line is not necessarily as hawkish as Netanyahu’s posture, since it suggests a willingness to consider diplomatic means of removing the group from power. Eisenkot has also strongly criticized Netanyahu’s campaign pledge to overthrow the Iranian regime. Instead, he supports measures to take the enriched uranium out of Iran and to put its nuclear program under a verification regime. “You can’t overthrow a government from the air; it’s a delusion,” he said. But he nonetheless backed bombing the country to weaken its military and nuclear program, even if he disagreed with the ultimate end.

The rest of the world, of course, does not share Israel’s view. Quite the contrary—in the wake of the destruction of Gaza, polls show that Israel’s international approval ratings have hit new lows. Politicians in every region are arguing that Israel is guilty of major human rights violations, with many claiming that the country has committed genocide. Even some of Israel’s friends are warning that the state has gone overboard. In July 2025, for example, U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer declared that although Israel “has a right to defend itself and end Hamas’s brutal rule,” the “reporting and images out of Gaza—depicting the devastating levels of hunger, starvation, suffering and death—are wholly unacceptable.”

Outside countries are also particularly furious about its settlement expansion in the West Bank, which cannot be justified as a reaction to October 7. As a result, sanctions have reached Israel’s shores. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband declared on September 8 that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank is unlawful and announced a sanctions regime against the settlements and companies involved in their financing and construction. Given that London is a major financial center, Israeli banks—which are financing the major settlement projects—are now in trouble.

Across the Atlantic, Israel still has the support of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Netanyahu’s reelection campaign. But most of the Democratic Party’s politicians—and even many Republicans—now want to stop or limit U.S. aid and technology transfers to the Israel Defense Forces, citing the use of American munitions in the destruction of Gaza. Many prominent Democratic Party officials want to sanction the country, too. If Democrats take control of at least one house of Congress in the midterms, the United States could stop sending blank checks to Israel.

Israelis generally attribute such rising international anger to anti-Semitism instead of sincerely held concerns about the rights of Palestinians, Middle Eastern stability, or the proper allocation of military resources. But they are nonetheless aware of their growing isolation and fear that, after the election, they might get hit by what former Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak has called a “diplomatic tsunami.” This assessment is widely accepted in the mainstream media and by Netanyahu, who argues that only he—with his superior English skills—can stop such an onslaught, much as he maneuvered to stop the Biden administration from ever imposing real consequences on the country for its war in Gaza. The Israeli right wing has been arguing for many years, with justification, that Israel can continue its occupation and denial of civil rights to the Palestinians while manipulating the international community with hasbara (public diplomacy and lobbying). Eisenkot, by contrast, will try to win the world back by being upfront about what his country is willing to accept and then negotiating honestly—two things that Netanyahu has rarely done.

Eisenkot’s approach would likely win over more international partners, at least for a time, as did the leaders of two other former military chiefs, Barak and Yitzhak Rabin, who unseated Likud governments. Netanyahu has burned so many bridges with his parade of lies that Eisenkot would probably get an international grace period simply by virtue of his relative honesty. And Eisenkot might indeed make changes that please Israel’s partners, such as slowing settlement construction. He opposes the controversial E1 settlement project, which is aimed at slicing a future Palestinian state by half, and has pledged to tackle Jewish terrorism.

But eventually, Eisenkot would disappoint any overseas Israel supporters who expect a thorough reversal of Netanyahu’s foreign and Palestinian policies. And even if he somehow changed his own mind on Palestinian statehood—which he insists he has never supported—his freedom of action would be severely restricted by his governing coalition. Eisenkot’s power bloc relies on two right-wing parties whose leaders strongly oppose the two-state solution and mistrust the Palestinians. One of them, Avigdor Lieberman, even wants to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and bring in Jordan to rule over the Palestinians who reside in the West Bank (an idea that Amman rejected decades ago). They would bring Eisenkot’s government down if he expressed openness to a Palestinian state.

Polling shows that the October 27 election will be extremely tight. In fact, if the surveys are right, neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu will win an outright majority. The country is thus likely to experience a period of horse-trading, as both politicians jockey to peel off the other’s partners. Netanyahu might even try to lure Eisenkot himself into a kind of unity government, promising to put his judicial overhaul or other culture-war campaigns on hold in return. (Eisenkot has adamantly rejected the idea of serving under Netanyahu, even for a rotation, but about-faces have been a staple of Israeli coalition politics.) Alternatively, negotiations could fail, and the country would almost immediately return to the polls. It would not be the first time that an Israeli contest failed to produce a lasting government: the country held five general elections from 2019 to 2022 before its political leaders established a coalition that could hold on to power for more than 12 months.

But no matter the outcome—a Netanyahu caretaker government, a Netanyahu majority government, a unity government, a minority Eisenkot cabinet supported by the Arab parties, or even an Eisenkot majority government—Israel’s next prime minister will keep occupying parts of its neighbors and brutalizing the Palestinians. He will thus have to contend with Israel’s increasing isolation from the rest of the world. The government might end up spending even more on local arms production to replace U.S.-funded systems, working hard to bypass export controls on military and dual-use items (as sanctioned Iran and Russia do today, and as Israel did in its early years). Israel might face its ultimate fear—losing the United States’ veto at the UN Security Council, which has protected its occupation since 1967 from international censure, even under critical Democratic presidents such as Jimmy Carter and Barack Obama.

This may not be the outcome that Israelis actually want. But without a sea change in how they think about their problems, it is the one they are careening toward. The odds, however, are particularly pronounced if Netanyahu and his partners stay in power. In that case, more liberal Israelis will not wait to see how badly the world punishes their country. They will instead flee to pursue their way of life in a quieter place.

#5974. Redistricting efforts blow up in Republicans' faces amid historic House losses

Fox News provides live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results as the Democratic Party regained control of both congressional chambers.

Republicans' gambit to stave off election losses by changing congressional maps backfired in most of the country on Tuesday night.

Democrats swept both battleground House seats and areas considered safe GOP territory in an unprecedented midterm election performance, despite the best efforts by Republican-led states to redistrict in multiple states to give their party an edge.

"It was definitely the wrong move," one House Republican told Fox News Digital. "One of the truisms in politics is never to overreach. We did and that was part of the reason for the backlash."

DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott arrives during a press conference for Eli Lilly and Company in Houston on Sept. 23, 2025. (Antranik Tavitian/Reuters)

Republicans in states that were particularly affected by redistricting had been warning their governors for months that it could be a bad idea, another person told Fox News Digital.

"It's a bridge too far, and clearly the bridge blew up behind them," that person said.

In Texas, where the GOP-led state government altered the congressional map to give Republicans an advantage in five districts, Democrats are projected to win at least three.

Reps. Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas, and Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, managed to hold onto their seats despite Republicans' efforts, and Democrats also won the newly redrawn 35th Congressional District. The remaining two have not been called.

Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, during a House Subcommittee on Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies hearing in Washington, D.C., on May 21, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Florida Republicans are on pace to lose all four House seats they drew to favor their party. Incumbent Reps. Kathy Castor, D-Fla., and Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., are projected to win their respective altered districts, along with political newcomer Pia Dandiya in her red-leaning seat.

Rep. Darren Soto, D-Fla., who was expected to be hardest-hit by Sunshine State Republicans' efforts, is narrowly leading in a race that's still too close to call.

Overall, however, it's worth noting that Florida was a bright spot for the GOP overall on Tuesday night. Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., won the race for governor, and all Republican incumbents kept their seats.

Meanwhile, a push in Ohio to make districts held by Reps. Greg Landsman, D-Ohio, and Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, more favorable to Republicans, also failed.

And in Alabama, Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., won another term despite his seat also being altered to favor Republicans.

Gov. Ron DeSantis holds a press conference at the State Emergency Operations Center regarding Hurricane Isaias on Oct. 8, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters)

The process of redistricting is traditionally done after a national census, to account for population shifts in each state.

Changing congressional maps mid-decade is a controversial move that saw bipartisan pushback — though both sides ultimately took part.

On the left, California Gov. Gavin Newsom led his state through a referendum where voters chose to give the legislature the ability to change its own congressional map to give Democrats an edge where, it appears so far, they have one.

#5973. House GOP races to lock down new leadership after blue wave

A sweeping tide of Democratic wins Tuesday left Republicans preparing for a new face atop the House GOP leadership ranks as the party gears up to defend President Donald Trump from a list of investigations.

It’s shaping up to be a battle between sitting Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, pitting two lawmakers Trump has publicly praised against one another.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana had been trying to stay the course before Republicans dropped a stunning amount of seats, including ones considered deep-red. The cascade of losses, which will give Democrats a sizable majority in the 435-member chamber, forced Johnson to stand down. He told his staff on a Wednesday morning call he would not seek the minority leader job for the next Congress when the GOP conference votes behind closed doors next week.

In a possible sign of what’s to come when the often-raucous conference meets to hear from candidates and vote, some GOP insiders were split Wednesday on which lawmaker should take over as leader.

“It might be Jordan’s for the taking. I think the real fight will be at whip and conference chair,” said one GOP source with ties to each member’s office, granted anonymity to be candid.

In a letter to colleagues Jordan circulated Wednesday, he pitched himself as “battle-tested on the oversight front,” which could help as Democrats go full-tilt on probing the Trump administration. “For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democrat majority,” Jordan’s letter reads.

But another person familiar with Scalise’s thinking said “his No. 1 goal will be to lead the conference back into the majority,” describing Scalise as a “proven and tested leader who is ready on day one.”

“The conference knows him, how he fights, and that he’s a trusted leader,” the person said.

Spokespersons for Scalise and Johnson did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment on their plans.

Heading into the midterms, it appeared Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the sitting majority whip, had been working behind the scenes to shore up his standing with House GOP members in a bid to become the No. 2 Republican in January.

Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger of Texas has also pitched himself for minority whip, writing in a Wednesday letter to colleagues that he believed his conference needed “fresh ideas” and had “missed many opportunities.”

The scope of Tuesday’s losses had some calling for a completely clean slate, with Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., posting a message on social media to House and Senate brass: “Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction.”

“Having Jordan and Emmer in as leadership won’t be much of a change at the top,” the first GOP source said. “But President Trump should want a warrior like Jordan with impeachment experience in charge, given the Democrats will inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

To that end, Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, likely the incoming House Judiciary Committee chairman, said in a brief interview before the chamber adjourned in September to campaign that “there’s a long list of potentially impeachable offenses” to look at from the president, his family members and inner circle.

An aggressive investigatory push by Democrats could make Jordan, in Trump’s eyes, an attractive candidate to lead the conference. Jordan fought hard against Trump’s two first-term impeachments, including with fiery cable news hits that were praised by the TV-focused chief executive.

Whatever happens, it will cap off a rocky ride for Johnson, who claimed the gavel in the tumultuous weeks after Kevin McCarthy was ousted as speaker in October 2023.

In a statement released early Wednesday morning, Johnson did not reveal his next move.

“While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning. This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history,” Johnson said. “However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world.”

Notably, during a phone interview with Politico late Tuesday night, Trump was asked about Johnson — but did not endorse him for minority leader.

“I think he’s done a very good job,” the president said, his voice hoarse from an October-long rally blitz that did not pay off for his party. “I mean, they’re going to have to make that decision. He’s going to have to make that decision. But he’s a good person and a good man.”

On Wednesday Trump told reporters at the White House he intended to stay out of the coming House GOP leadership race.

While Republicans are eager to avoid repeating the bitter public battles of the past, the fight for minority leader is in some ways a rerun. Both Scalise and Jordan tried for the speaker’s gavel back in 2023 after McCarthy’s sacking but neither landed the job.

A former high school and college wrestler who later coached grappling, Jordan was once considered too much of a firebrand to lead the entire caucus.

“Early on he wasn’t really given the opportunity to show what he’s capable of because of his steadfast conservative positions,” Ray Yonkura, who was Jordan’s chief of staff for a decade and has done political work for him, told CQ Roll Call in October 2023. “He was oftentimes pushed to the side, or different Republican leaders tried to keep him down.”

“Once he was given an opportunity to show what he’s capable of, I think a lot of people realized that this is somebody whose skill set can actually be good in a leadership role,” Yonkura said then.

Jordan has faced questions over the years about what he knew about sexual abuse by a doctor at The Ohio State University when he worked there as an assistant wrestling coach starting in the 1980s. He has repeatedly denied knowing of the abuse, and multiple Republicans told CQ Roll Call in 2023 that it hadn’t factored into their support for Jordan.

As for Scalise, he went through a public ordeal in 2017 when he was shot by a gunman at a GOP baseball practice, sustaining serious injuries. He later was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, and in 2024 said he was in remission.

Beyond the House leadership shuffle ahead of the start of the 120th Congress, G. William Hoagland, a former Senate GOP leadership aide, said there would be a broader battle among Republicans as they analyze their losses and look ahead to 2028.

“I take Steve Bannon’s comment recently seriously that the Republican Party will be engulfed in a civil war over the future of the party,” he said, referring to recent comments from Trump’s former chief 2016 campaign and White House strategist. “Expect that civil war to play out over the next couple of weeks in the midst of all the other legislative issues they have to deal with in the lame-duck session.”

Niels Lesniewski, Savannah Behrmann, Paul Krawczak and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#5972. U.S. Democracy Is Back—Sort of

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: U.S. Democracy Is Back—Sort of

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The message of the 2026 midterm elections is decidedly in: U.S. democracy is not dead, not by a long shot.

There is, at long last, the glimmer of a beginning to the end of President Donald Trump’s decade-long dominance of national politics. Most of all, the 2028 presidential race—which effectively begins today—is now up in the air. So is the ultimate direction of the country’s international role, which will be decided by that election.

The message of the 2026 midterm elections is decidedly in: U.S. democracy is not dead, not by a long shot.

There is, at long last, the glimmer of a beginning to the end of President Donald Trump’s decade-long dominance of national politics. Most of all, the 2028 presidential race—which effectively begins today—is now up in the air. So is the ultimate direction of the country’s international role, which will be decided by that election.

But no one should kid themselves that the next two years are going to be anything other than ugly, chaotic, and brutal. Both Democrats and Republicans will be engaged in vicious infighting over fundamental policy issues, whether the question is the survival of the international order, engagement with allies and adversaries alike, immigration policy, or tariffs and the strength of the economy.

Above all, it’s important to note that even with the dramatic turnover in Congress—with Democrats taking back both the House and Senate in decisive fashion—the president has shown very little inclination to defer to Congress, or even to the courts, on any issue that involves foreign or domestic policy.

That Trumpian defiance will continue, whether the question is finding a way to end his prolonged Iran war on palatable terms, force a resolution to Russia’s nearly five-year-long invasion of Ukraine, persist in his crackdown on immigrants, or continue to unilaterally impose tariffs on whomever he pleases. In an Election Day interview with CBS News, Trump declared that even if the Democrats take control, he is prepared to use “tremendous” executive power to push through his agenda. “I have the ultimate power—it’s called ‘veto,’” he said.

Trump also has the power of the executive order. In less than two years, he has signed 292 executive orders, 90 memoranda, and 192 proclamations, touching critical policies from voting rights to the reversal of 80 years of trade policy.

But facts are a stubborn thing. In his second term, the economic news was so grim and Trump’s abuse of power so brazen—he pushed the Justice Department to prosecute his enemies, enriched his family, and launched a costly war with no legal basis—that even many of those voters who supported him two years ago could no longer look away. In the weeks leading up to the vote, Trump’s approval ratings fell to historic lows. The result was an equally historic rebuke, one so profound that even deeply red states turned against Trump. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico won the Senate race and State Rep. Gina Hinojosa was elected as the first Democratic governor in 32 years. Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas in 94 years.

“The system is working,” said Charles Kupchan of the Council on Foreign Relations, author of the new book, Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come. “Voters have held accountable a president who has been failing to deliver on virtually all fronts.”

But Kupchan added: “Democratic control of Congress will have virtually no impact on Trump’s foreign policy. He has largely disregarded the preferences of the legislature on matters of statecraft—and will certainly continue to do so with Congress in the hands of Democrats.  On domestic policy, expect confrontation, paralysis, and a swirl of investigations.”

Still, it’s clear that as a political force, Trump is badly damaged—no doubt permanently as he finishes out his last term at the age of 80. The president brazenly made the midterm election a referendum about himself. “Pretend I’m on the ballot,” he said frequently in the weeks before the election. Following Tuesday’s devastating vote, however, the rebuffed president reversed course. He suggested the problem was not him but the flawed candidates the GOP put forward, including the corruption-plagued Ken Paxton in Texas (whom Trump had endorsed in the primary) and the  fumbling Darline Graham in South Carolina (whom Trump had recommended). Both went down to defeat.

“I wasn’t on the ballot and, if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE,” Trump posted on Truth Social late Tuesday night as the Republican defeat took shape.

Republicans successfully connected wartime spending to the rising price of pork chops.

The president’s hold on national politics finally gave way Tuesday.

Trump also backed away from threats of declaring voter fraud the way he did after his 2020 defeat in the presidential election, telling the New York Times that he is “absolutely willing” to accept the results. Of Democrats, he said, “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.”

Trump is clearly concerned about his legacy. Now he and his GOP successors will have to address the fracturing of the MAGA coalition that returned Trump to the White House in 2024.

And following Tuesday’s election, it’s fair to say that that coalition no longer exists.

In 2024, Trump exploited an inflationary environment under President Joe Biden and the seeming takeover of the Democratic Party by progressive, so-called woke issues—not to mention a degree of misogyny and racism directed at Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democratic candidate—to win over formerly Democratic leaning blue-collar voters, especially Latino and Black men. Together with his neo-isolationist MAGA base, that was enough to put him over the edge against Harris.

But earlier this year, Trump inflicted a catastrophic double wound on himself by launching an ill-justified war against Iran. In doing so he simultaneously alienated many middle-income voters who have been hammered by rising prices spiked by the war—as well as disenchanted MAGA voters who feel betrayed over his previous promises to avoid foreign wars and restore the economy.

Many Latino voters who went heavily Democratic in Tuesday’s election also appeared to be alienated by Trump’s broad crackdown on immigrants, especially since the dragnet has pulled in some legal residents.

Trump was rebuffed across the board by many of these voters. As Politico’s Playbook noted, “The cross-country transformation of the Latino voting electorate will go down as one of the biggest stories of the night. From a full sweep in Texas’ Mexican-American Rio Grande Valley to Pennsylvania’s Puerto Rican-dominated Lehigh Valley to even Dem gains in heavily Puerto Rican, Cuban, Venezuelan and Colombian central and south Florida, all showed the same direction toward Democrats.”

Looking ahead to 2028, many of those newly alienated former Trump voters will be up for grabs. The question is whether a badly divided Democratic Party will be in a position to draw them in.

“The biggest challenge for Democrats will be to unite around a platform focused on health insurance, housing, and industrial policies geared to fostering inclusive growth, labor-market transformation for the AI economy, and assistance for those who will bear the costs of the transition,” said Ian Shapiro, a political scientist at Yale University. “They should pass bill after bill on these issues, even if Trump vetoes them all. They will become the basis for their Project 2029, which serious contenders for the Democratic presidential nomination will have to embrace.”

And yet the Democrats show little sign of doing that. The new slate in the House and Senate consists of a large ideological spread of legislators ranging from moderates to left-wing populists who are aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America. Prominent among them: the senator-elect from Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate. And before it settles on a 2028 nominee, the party will be engulfed in big fights over taxes, healthcare, and foreign policy, especially support for Israel.

This post appeared in FP's The Reading List newsletter. Sign up here.

Michael Hirsh is a columnist for Foreign Policy. He is the author of two books: Capital Offense: How Washington’s Wise Men Turned America’s Future Over to Wall Street and At War With Ourselves: Why America Is Squandering Its Chance to Build a Better World. X: @michaelphirsh

Florida Governor-elect Byron Donalds told Fox News on Wednesday that he believes Americans' frustrations about gas and diesel prices "boiled over" against Republicans on Election Day.

The Trump-backed Florida House Republican made the remark after being asked by "Fox & Friends" co-host Brian Kilmeade why he thinks so many people were unhappy with the first two years of the president's second term. "I think, look, when you talk to people on the ground, gas prices are a major problem. I think people were looking at the price of gas, the price of diesel, and I think those frustrations boiled over," Donalds said.

"I think if you not just look in Florida, but look around the country, what I'm starting to see is that we have a lot of Republicans who either did not vote or decided to go and vote for Democrats. "And that's something I'll be talking about with my colleagues on Capitol Hill when I get back during this lame duck session. We're also going to be laser-focused on that here in Florida moving forward."

#5968. The New Energy Stalemate in Ukraine

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

TATIANA MITROVA is a Global Fellow at the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University.

SERGEY VAKULENKO is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin.

Why Russia’s Escalating Attacks Are Unlikely to End the War

In the days since U.S. President Donald Trump’s highly public falling out with Ukraine and growing rapprochement with Russia, Kyiv’s prospects going into the fifth winter of war look grim. The Trump administration has demanded that Ukraine suspend its attacks on Russian refineries, which have been one of Ukraine’s most effective means of putting pressure on Moscow. Meanwhile, Kyiv faces dangerous gaps in its air defenses against Russia’s jet-powered drones and stepped-up use of ballistic missiles. And Trump has entered into a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that temporarily waives U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports, offering Moscow a diplomatic win. Trump’s envoys have also proposed that Europe increase purchases of Russian gas as part of an effort to gain the Kremlin’s support for peace—further complicating the efforts of Ukraine and its remaining allies to squeeze Russia.

Yet missing from this bleak picture are the ways that Ukraine has already adapted to escalating attacks. Kyiv has developed innovative strategies to mitigate the impact of Russian energy strikes and keep its grid running, even amid intense bombardment. And despite the new U.S. pressure, Ukraine has continued to launch powerful drone strikes against Russia’s energy infrastructure, including successful mid-October attacks on an oil terminal in St. Petersburg and industrial gas processing plants as far away as Surgut and the Novy Urengoy, 1,800 miles from the Ukrainian border. Overall, since mid-2025, Ukrainian drone strikes have reduced Russian refinery throughput by roughly 30 percent; they have also eroded a significant share of Moscow’s excess refining capacity, resulting in a gasoline shortfall of about ten percent.

Still, this is only one part of a rapidly evolving energy war. Moscow has developed its own ways to limit the effects of Ukrainian strikes. And it has intensified its assault on Ukrainian infrastructure, including an October 19 barrage that damaged more than ten energy facilities. DiXi Group, a Ukrainian think tank, has estimated that Russia launched 12,800 missiles and drones at Ukrainian energy facilities in 2025 and early 2026, compared with just 2,800 during the first three years of the war combined. Although these figures count launches rather than successful strikes, they show how massive and relentless the Russian campaign has become.

Moreover, both sides are now able to target the substitutes and reserves that in the past could be used to cushion losses. Following Russian strikes on local power plants in early October, Ukrainians experienced widespread blackouts, even though Ukraine’s national grid had electricity to spare, because Russia continued hitting the lines and substations carrying the reserve power. During the summer, Ukraine hit so many of the refineries and pipelines around Moscow that Russia was forced to bring fuel by rail from as far as Lake Baikal, thousands of miles away.

If U.S. pressure and negotiations cannot stop the energy war, the central question for Ukraine is whether its remarkable capacity to adapt can keep pace with Russian attacks. At the same time, its fortunes this winter will depend on whether it can continue to hit Russian infrastructure in ways that challenge Moscow’s ability to repair and rebuild. Both Russia and Ukraine must now protect and repair their entire national networks around the clock; attackers can concentrate on the most vulnerable sites and strike again as soon as repairs are done. In such a war, defensive ingenuity matters as much as offensive capability. In the end, energy attacks alone are unlikely to force either side to accept the other’s terms, neither side may be able to gain a decisive advantage, even as both incur mounting costs. Recognizing the limits, as well as the power, of these strikes may be crucial not only to ending the present conflict but also to understanding the role that energy infrastructure will likely play in future wars.

For Ukraine, international support has been especially crucial in containing Russia’s energy barrage. As of November 2025, before the worst of last winter’s attacks, Ukraine had suffered $17.1 billion in direct damage to its electricity infrastructure, according to a report by the UN, the World Bank, and the European Commission. Yet Kyiv was able to keep the electricity flowing by drawing on the country’s remaining nuclear plants; repairing thermal generation facilities; increasing electricity, gas, and diesel imports; and compensating for lost power plants with distributed generation—smaller units running on solar, wind, gas, and diesel energy that are connected to the main grid.

Europe has also provided crucial replacement technology. In 2025, the European Commission delivered equipment from a retired Lithuanian thermal power plant to Ukraine in 149 shipments, enabling Ukraine to provide power to one million people. Such transfers have turned foreign utilities and suppliers into part of Ukraine’s rapid repair system. In September, Ukraine and the UN Development Program launched a new coordination center to speed up the installation of donated energy equipment.

Expanded use of batteries and distributed power also play a growing role. In September 2025, the Ukrainian energy company DTEK and the U.S.-based battery maker Fluence installed battery storage at six sites around Kyiv and Dnipro, with enough capacity to supply 600,000 households, roughly half of Kyiv, for two hours. Meanwhile, Kyiv has put in place 150 megawatts of distributed power generation—not enough to cover winter peak demand, but sufficient to provide more than half of the city’s essential services, including water supplies, hospitals, and heating systems. Nonetheless, Ukrainian reports suggest that 2,500 to 3,000 of Kyiv’s 12,000 apartment buildings could enter winter without an alternative heat supply.

That vulnerability is especially dangerous because restoring electricity does not automatically restore heat. Replacement boilers can help, but they must be installed locally, supplied with fuel, and connected to functioning heat networks, often while the same city remains under repeated attack. Last winter, UN monitors recorded at least 74 Russian attacks on heating infrastructure across Ukraine—attacks that left hundreds of thousands of people without heat or hot water for weeks on end in frigid temperatures. Keeping the national electric grid running did not make those homes habitable in freezing weather. Residents can try to solve the problem with electric space heaters, but their widespread use could overload the already fragile grid.

To prepare for even worse conditions this winter, Kyiv has been building up gas reserves. As of August, Ukraine’s gas stocks stood at 13.1 billion cubic meters, compared with 9.6 billion a year earlier. Still, stored gas must reach functioning heat and power plants, and electricity must pass through functioning transmission networks, both of which Russia has been continually attacking. Regardless of how resilient the national system is, Russia’s incessant targeting of particular Ukrainian cities has left them exposed, because local sources of substitute supply are often attacked before damaged facilities can be restored.

Meanwhile, Ukrainians are paying for the survival of their energy system in ways that capacity measures miss. Across the country, businesses have to run expensive generators, cut shifts, or close. Households spend more for fewer hours of reliable service. Declining industrial demand can make the electricity balance sheet look healthier, when the reality is that the economy is deteriorating under the pressure of relentless attacks. Those losses weaken the tax base and increase the need for foreign support. Russia does not have to switch off Ukraine’s power to impose an extraordinary burden.

Russia has also felt the growing effects of the energy war. In theory, Moscow has a much larger cushion: when the war began, its refineries produced more fuel than its domestic market consumed, and many had excess capacity to distill crude than to convert the resulting streams into finished motor fuel. Losing one distillation unit did not necessarily mean losing an equivalent share of gasoline or diesel supply. But Ukraine’s attacks this year have tested the limits of that flexibility.

In June, Ukrainian drones hit one of two processing units at Moscow’s Kapotnya refinery and hit the other six days later. The refinery was shut down after the June attacks and although it subsequently resumed operations, another strike again halted processing in September. Elsewhere, Ukrainian attacks have damaged complex units that are designed to raise fuel yields and improve quality; they can take six to eight months to fix, so they might remain unavailable through the coming winter heating season. Spare primary distillation capacity cannot replace damaged secondary equipment needed to turn intermediate products into finished gasoline and diesel.

To make up for these losses, the Russian government has loosened fuel standards, allowing naphtha blended with octane boosters to enter the gasoline supply, and extended state subsidies to imported gasoline. Russian companies can also send crude to its ally Belarus for processing or import finished products. These measures have helped fill consumers’ gas tanks without restoring the equipment that previously supplied them. But they come at a cost, which consumers, companies, and the state will all ultimately have to absorb.

Not all Ukrainian drone strikes have had such long-term impact. In March 2026, for example, Ukraine attacked the Ust-Luga oil terminal, which is on the Baltic Sea near St. Petersburg, continually for almost two weeks, halting oil shipments from that terminal. But shipments from Ust-Luga resumed a few weeks later, and by late April Russia’s total seaborne crude exports averaged 3.8 million barrels a day—up seven percent from March and 11 percent from a year earlier. This increase helped offset falling exports of refined products, as damage to refineries left more crude available for export.

For Moscow, the most pressing question is how to manage fuel shortages. Through higher prices and rationing, it can ensure that the military remains well supplied even if civilians have to cut back. It can also use subsidies and price controls to provide some relief to consumers. None of these options are costless, but as long as the government is willing to impose lower living standards and absorb the resulting political costs, it retains considerable room to maneuver. Ukrainian strikes can force Russia to spread its air defense thinner, absorb money and labor, and reduce its income from refining. They can somewhat reduce the oil and gas revenue that finances Russia’s war, but none of these costs are likely to make the war prohibitively expensive for the Kremlin.

Paradoxically, the growing success of Ukraine’s strikes against Russian refineries has brought new pressure on Kyiv itself. To buttress its increasingly constrained domestic market, Russia has reduced the amount of diesel it is selling abroad. Normally, higher prices should encourage refiners elsewhere to take up the slack, but the U.S. war against Iran has made that adjustment harder. Combined Russian and Middle Eastern net diesel and gasoil exports in September were 1.3 million barrels a day below their level a year earlier, according to the International Energy Agency. That global supply crunch has also affected the United States, which has now blamed Ukraine for stubbornly high U.S. diesel prices.

Ordinarily, the United States enjoys a substantial diesel surplus and is the world’s largest diesel exporter. Yet in the absence of export controls, quotas, or export tariffs, the U.S. market is exposed to galloping international prices, even when there is no U.S. fuel shortage. It is also far easier for the Trump administration to press Ukraine to stop its attacks on Russian refineries—and to enter a diesel agreement with Russia—than to restore lost Middle Eastern diesel exports.

In reality, Washington’s moves are unlikely to add much to global supply in the near term: redirecting existing exports does not create additional fuel. A larger, lasting increase would require Russian refineries to recover and stay in operation. This is where Washington has an incentive to restrain Ukraine’s attacks—even to the point of withholding, or threatening to withhold, Kyiv’s access to Starlink satellite service or U.S. intelligence, or to block European purchases of U.S. weapons for Ukraine. If Ukraine complies with U.S. demands, one risk is that Moscow could obtain protection for its refineries while continuing its assault on Ukrainian cities.

The United States is not the only external player in this widening energy war. For Europe, Ukraine’s collapse would create a security threat far greater than the cost of replacing transformers or financing fuel imports. Thus, in mid-October, the EU’s ambassador to Ukraine described a $1.1 billion energy support package Europe is preparing for the coming winter, which will enhance Ukraine’s ability to recover. But if some European countries, despite the European Commission’s opposition, accede to the Trump administration’s proposal to expand European purchases of Russian gas in the hope of lowering energy costs for households and industry—that could bolster Moscow’s earnings and its ability to finance the war. Europe’s energy choices matter on both sides of the contest.

China and India may also affect the future direction of the energy war. Thus far, both countries’ purchases of Russian crude have helped sustain Russia’s war machine. Moreover, by refining discounted barrels of Russian crude, both countries can benefit their own industries, and by exporting more refined fuel, they can ease the global crunch that is now driving U.S. pressure on Ukraine. But the ability of these countries to raise their exports depends on available crude and government approval—particularly in China. Over time, Russia’s leverage from the current diesel crunch will shrink as other suppliers recover, trade adjusts, and consumption falls. But that shift is unlikely to happen in time for this winter: the International Energy Agency expects diesel markets to remain tight well into 2027.

For both Russia and Ukraine, the aim of the energy war is clear: to disrupt or break the adversary’s economy to the point of undermining support for the war or making it unsustainable. But there are few indications that either side can achieve such an outcome. U.S. pressure could nevertheless produce a cease-fire or a broader settlement, even on terms deeply unfavorable to Ukraine. A mutual halt to energy strikes would give both sides relief and time to recover.

For now, however, an enormous gap remains between the conditions that Moscow and Kyiv deem minimally acceptable for even a temporary cease-fire. High levels of mutual distrust have increased that gap further. Moreover, a deal to protect only refineries, as the Trump administration has called for, would leave Ukraine’s cities and other infrastructure still exposed to Russian attacks. And Moscow has less incentive to accept any such deal if it can secure Ukrainian restraint through pressure by Washington, without making concessions of its own.

If diplomacy fails, the most likely scenario is another winter of sustained strikes on energy and other infrastructure by both sides. For Russia, the loss of refining capacity has been manageable thus far, but that does not preclude larger problems ahead. With each additional loss of capacity, Russia’s protection of its military energy supply becomes more expensive. Certain regions that have already been squeezed, such as occupied Crimea, could become especially vulnerable. If Moscow is unable to make repairs fast enough or otherwise compensate for further losses of refining capacity, regional fuel shortages could develop into wider disruptions to civilian transport and industry.

For Ukraine, the central risk is a cascading series of Russian attacks on the same city. During prolonged cold, repeated attacks—whether on Kyiv or Kharkiv or Odessa—could exhaust backup supplies faster than crews can restore service. Prolonged pump stoppages could lead to a disastrous local scenario of ruptured water supply, district heating, and sewage pipes, even if electricity remains available elsewhere in the country. A milder winter and timely equipment deliveries could keep Ukraine ahead of such a crisis, but delays in air defense deliveries or the loss of a critical heating facility could overwhelm a city whose electricity balance looked adequate. An indication of danger will be local power outages that continue to grow despite repairs, showing that recovery is unable to keep pace with attacks.

As it prepares for what will likely be its harshest winter yet, Kyiv faces a dilemma: if it reduces or suspends its attacks on Russian refineries to preserve U.S. military support, it will give Moscow a repair window while the Ukrainian grid remains exposed. If Kyiv refuses, it could continue its strikes but face intelligence or Starlink cutoffs that could make its infrastructure harder to defend. An additional influx of European funds and technology could soften the consequences—and perhaps provide some alternatives to U.S. communication networks—but will not fully replace U.S. intelligence and air-defense capabilities. That dilemma will not go away as long as Ukraine’s own infrastructure is exposed to attack.

As it approaches its fifth anniversary, the conflict in Ukraine has transformed energy warfare in ways that have few precedents. The advent of cheap long-range weapons has allowed each side almost unlimited access to the energy infrastructure on which the other depends. Yet at the same time, innovations in distributed power generation, batteries, and mobile equipment have given defenders novel ways to preserve essential services and continually recover, even in the face of large-scale attacks. Russia’s deep industrial reserves and Ukraine’s impressive adaptation have shown that complex energy systems can withstand enormous damage. That endurance has been far greater than a tally of destroyed assets on either side would suggest.

But this same resilience can make wars longer and more devastating. As Ukraine and Russia have shown, each side can gain confidence from its ability to sustain repeated attacks while also persuading itself that an even more intense campaign against its adversary might finally succeed. In this dynamic, each adjustment and workaround by one side invites a fresh attack by the other, and each new strike accelerates the search for new ways to endure. This adaptation spiral can continue even as economic and human losses mount. Only a true cease-fire can break the cycle. And that will depend on political choices that energy attacks alone cannot determine.

How a True “Energy Cease-Fire” Can Curb Putin

How the Shadow Fleet Enables Russia’s Hybrid Warfare in Europe

Why Ukraine’s Campaign Against Moscow’s Energy Sector Is Working

Congress Should Wield Oil Sanctions to Force Russia to Negotiate

Washington Cannot Achieve Tech Dominance on Its Own

How Long Will Elites Stay Loyal to Kim Jong Un?

Why the Country’s Food Insecurity Could Prevent a War Over Taiwan

The Case for an Economic Security Alliance
